title: RedPhys: An Extensible Red-Teaming Platform for Physical-World Models and Agents
claim: A modular platform connects configurable components through shared interfaces into evaluation and reusable outputs, with slots for user extensions.
layout: 3 stacked tiers top-to-bottom, 4 module cards in top row, dashed add-slots

Tier (a), 'Configure the test', holds four cards side by side: Physical tasks, Test methods, Protection, and Models/agents. Each card has a small icon, a bold heading, short descriptive lines, and a dashed-outline 'Add ...' button that marks user extension slots. The '12 attack methods' line is highlighted in orange. caption: \textbf{Overview of \sys{}.} The platform connects physical-world tasks, test methods, protection, and PhyModels or PhyAgents through shared interfaces. Dashed "Add" slots denote user-defined extensions. Adversarial stress testing is the primary focus, with non-adversarial testing also supported. Outputs include robustness reports and reusable datasets of test cases, labels, and model responses for future alignment.
abstract: Physical-world models (PhyModels) perform grounded perception, reasoning, or decision tasks; physical-world agents (PhyAgents) combine these models with planning or tool use. We introduce RedPhys, an extensible red-teaming platform, instantiated here with vision-language models and agents. Shared interfaces make tasks, test methods, defenses, and victim systems configurable and extensible, producing robustness reports and datasets for future alignment. The platform emphasizes adversarial testing that seeks physically grounded functional failures, while also supporting non-adversarial input perturbations without an attack objective. The benchmark integrates 12 red-teaming methods, 3 model-agnostic defenses, and 13 PhyModels across seven physical domains under a practical black-box threat model. An agentic target-generation pipeline derives a scene-specific, physically grounded target, so targeted methods pursue the same intended error. Our evaluation shows that when attackers control the text prompt or add auxiliary visual instructions, injection exposes substantial instruction-following vulnerabilities; among bounded visual-transfer attacks, multimodal co-optimization transfers best; single-pass generative attacks approach iterative methods without per-image optimization; and neither model scale nor physical-reasoning post-training confers robustness. Code is available at https://github.com/loopleap-lab/RedPhys.
